title: Contains Duplicate
directAnswer: Return true if any value appears at least twice. The interview-grade answer is a single pass building a hash set: if the current value is already in the set, return true; otherwise add it. O(n) time, O(n) space. The sort-and-scan alternative is O(n log n) time but O(1) extra space — name it as the space-saving trade-off.

remember.formula:
seen = set()
for x in nums:
    if x in seen: return True
    seen.add(x)
return False
rules: Check membership **before** adding — otherwise every element 'matches itself'.
A **set**, not a map — you only need presence, not a value or a count.
Return early on the first repeat; don't scan the whole array if you don't have to.
If asked to do it in `O(1)` space, pivot to **sort then compare adjacent** (`O(n log n)`).
`len(set(nums)) != len(nums)` is the one-liner — fine to mention, but show the loop to prove you know the mechanics.

De-duplication, uniqueness checks, or first-repeat detection
antiSignals: Strict O(1) extra space required → sort then compare neighbours
Need the index/positions of the duplicate → use a hash map (value → index)
Need *counts* of each value → hash map, not a set
remember.takeaway: Whenever the question is 'have I seen this before?', a hash set turns the answer into an O(1) lookup. It's the simplest member of the same family as Two Sum, Longest Consecutive Sequence, and Group Anagrams.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for a hash set to trade space for time on a membership problem — and whether you can articulate the sort-based O(1)-space alternative.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Adding to the set before checking (so the first occurrence falsely matches itself), or using a heavyweight hash map when a set is enough.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State both solutions and their trade-off out loud: hash set is O(n)/O(n), sort-and-scan is O(n log n)/O(1). Ask whether memory or speed is the priority before committing.

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears **at least twice** in the array, and return `false` if every element is distinct.
understanding: Decide whether the array has any repeated value at all. We don't care *which* value repeats or *where* — just yes/no on the existence of a duplicate.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Assume no. If it were sorted, comparing adjacent elements is O(n) and O(1) space.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array be empty or have one element?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Constraints say length ≥ 1. A single element can't duplicate, so the answer is false there.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you need the duplicate value or just whether one exists?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just whether one exists — that's why a set suffices over a counting map.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is extra memory a concern?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If O(1) space is required, sort first and compare neighbours instead of using a set.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Compare Every Pair
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to anchor the complexity, then immediately offer something better.
hints: How would you check, with no extra data structures, whether two positions hold the same value?
Compare every pair (i, j) with j > i and return true the moment nums[i] == nums[j].
Two nested loops. It works but it's quadratic — that's your cue to look for a faster membership test.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n(n−1)/2 comparisons in the worst case (all distinct), no extra memory.
approaches.explanation:
Check every unordered pair of indices: for each `i`, walk every later `j > i` and test `nums[i] == nums[j]`. Return `true` on the first match, `false` if no pair ever matches.

**Why mention it at all.** It's the literal reading of 'does any value appear twice', and stating it shows you can establish a correctness baseline before optimizing. But with `n` up to `10⁵`, `n²/2 ≈ 5 × 10⁹` comparisons would time out — so this is a stepping stone, not the submission.
approaches.insight: Starting `j` at `i + 1` avoids comparing an element with itself and avoids re-checking the same pair in reverse. The quadratic cost comes from re-scanning; a hash set removes the re-scan by *remembering* what we've already seen.

approaches.name: Hash Set — One Pass (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'have I seen this value before?'.
hints: What data structure answers 'have I seen this exact value already?' in O(1) average time?
Scan left to right. Keep a set of values seen so far; for each value, check the set before adding.
If the value is already in the set you've found a duplicate — return true. Otherwise add it and continue.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass × O(1) average set operations = O(n) time. The set holds up to n elements → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain a hash set of values encountered so far. Walk the array once; for each value `x`, if `x` is already in the set, a duplicate exists so return `true`. Otherwise insert `x` and continue. If the loop finishes, every value was distinct, so return `false`.

**The shift from brute force.** Brute force re-scans the array for every element (quadratic). The set lets us replace 'scan everything before me' with a single O(1) membership query, because the set already *remembers* everything before the current index. We pay O(n) memory to make each check constant time.

**Why check before insert.** If we inserted `x` first and then checked membership, every element would find itself in the set and we'd return `true` immediately — even on a fully distinct array. The lookup must run against the set as it existed *before* this element.
approaches.insight: This is the minimal form of the 'remember what you've seen' trade that powers Two Sum and Longest Consecutive Sequence. A set (not a map) is the right tool because we only need presence — no associated value or count.

pitfalls: Inserting before checking — every element matches itself, always returns true.
Using a HashMap with dummy values where a HashSet is clearer and lighter.
Forgetting that sorting (the O(1)-space alternative) mutates the input — clone if the caller needs order preserved.

commonMistakes: Adding to the set before checking membership — returns true even on a distinct array.
Reaching for O(n²) nested loops when a one-pass set is trivial.
Assuming the input is sorted and only comparing neighbours without sorting first.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Insert-before-check (false positive)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you add the element first, the very next membership test finds it, so even a fully distinct array reports a duplicate.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting without copying when order matters
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The O(1)-space variant sorts in place, which destroys the caller's array ordering. Sort a copy if the original must be preserved.
